THE NIGHT THAT LORCA COMES SHALL BE A STRANGE NIGHT IN THE SOUTH, IT SHALL BE THE TIME WHEN NEGROES LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, GREEN TRAINS SHALL ARRIVE FROM RED PLANET MARS CRACKLING BLUENESS SHALL SEND TOOTH-COVERED CARS FOR THEM TO LEAVE IN, TO GO INTO THE NORTH FOREVER, AND I SEE MY LITTLE GIRL MOTHER AGAIN WITH HER CROSS THAT IS NOT BURNING, HER SKIRTS OF BLACK, OF ALL COLORS, HER AURA OF FAMILIARITY. THE SOUTH SHALL WEEP BITTER TEARS TO NO AVAIL, THE NEGROES HAVE GONE INTO CRACKLING BLUENESS. CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL ARRIVE WITH THE BOSTON COMMONS, TO TAKE ELISSI LANDI NORTH, CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL BE LAYING ON BOSTON COMMONS, ELISSI LANDI SHALL FEEL ALIVE AGAIN. THE WHITE SOUTH SHALL GATHER AT PRESERVATION HALL.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: THE, NIGHT, THAT

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, preserving its surreal imagery and original meaning while refining the flow and punctuation:

---

The night that Lorca comes shall be a strange night in the South—it shall be the hour when Negroes leave the South forever. Green trains shall arrive from the red planet Mars; a crackling blueness shall send tooth-covered cars to carry them away, into the North, forever. And I see my little girl-mother again, with her cross that does not burn, her skirts of black, of every color, her aura of familiarity.

The South shall weep bitter tears, to no avail—the Negroes have gone into the crackling blueness. Crispus Attucks shall arrive with the Boston Commons, to take Elissi Landi north. Crispus Attucks shall lie upon the Boston Commons; Elissi Landi shall feel alive again. I shall call her name as she steps onto the Boston Commons and flies north forever. Lincoln shall be there, to see them leave the South forever. Elissi Landi—she will be green.

The white South shall gather at Preservation Hall.

---

I maintained the prophetic, incantatory tone and surreal juxtapositions (trains from Mars, tooth-covered cars, the mythic figures) while smoothing transitions and adding punctuation for clarity and rhythm. Let me know if you'd like a version that leans more toward free verse formatting, or one that stays even closer to the original capitalization and cadence.
outputs.L2:
When Lorca arrives, the South will experience an unusual night—the moment black people depart the region permanently. Emerald-colored trains will descend from the crimson planet Mars, and a crackling blue force will dispatch tooth-adorned vehicles to carry them away, bound for the North for all time. In this vision, I behold my young girl-mother once more, bearing her unlit cross, wearing skirts of black that somehow contain every color, radiating an aura of deep familiarity.

The South's weeping will change nothing—its bitter tears will fall in vain, for the black population has already vanished into that crackling blue radiance. Crispus Attucks will appear alongside the Boston Common itself, arriving to escort Elissi Landi northward. He will rest upon that historic ground while she experiences a renewed sense of vitality. I will speak her name as she moves onto the Common and takes flight toward the North forever. Lincoln himself will be present, bearing witness to this eternal departure from the South, and Elissi Landi will take on a green hue.

Meanwhile, the white South will convene at Preservation Hall.
outputs.L3:
The poem conjures a night unlike any other—one charged with apocalyptic and mythic significance—heralded by the arrival of Federico García Lorca, whose presence signals a rupture in ordinary time. This is the night when Black people will finally and forever leave the South, their departure enacted not through conventional means but through fantastical vehicles: green trains arriving from Mars and strange "tooth-covered cars" bound for the North. The imagery collapses the historical reality of the Great Migration into a surreal, almost science-fictional register, suggesting that this exodus is cosmic in scale, part of some larger, otherworldly design rather than a mere sociological movement.

Within this fevered vision, the narrator conjures a deeply personal image: his mother, rendered as a "little girl," reappearing before him. She carries with her a cross that does not burn—an unmistakable inversion of the South's own symbols of racial terror—alongside skirts patterned in black and vivid, multicolored hues. She emanates a "familiar aura," a sensory recognition that grounds the poem's cosmic sweep in intimate, embodied memory. In this moment, personal history and universal myth become inseparable; the mother figure stands as both individual memory and archetype, her unburning cross a quiet act of defiance against the violence historically associated with such imagery in the South.

The South itself is personified as a grieving, bitter entity, weeping at the loss it cannot prevent. Yet its sorrow is impotent against the tide of departure: the Negroes it once bound do not simply leave but vanish, dissolving into what the poem calls "crackling blueness"—an image that suggests both electric transformation and transcendence, as though the act of leaving transmutes the travelers into something elemental, beyond the South's grasp entirely.

Historical and cultural figures populate this liminal night as well. Crispus Attucks, the first martyr of the American Revolution and a man of Black and Indigenous descent, arrives accompanied by the Boston Commons itself, as if history's landmarks and its heroes converge to escort the actress Elissi Landi northward. Her journey is framed as a kind of resurrection: she "will feel alive again" only once she reaches the North, and upon arrival, she undergoes a final metamorphosis—turning green, an image that echoes the green trains and reinforces the poem's recurring motif of transformation through migration.

Even Abraham Lincoln, the president associated with emancipation, is summoned to bear witness to this final, mythic departure from the South, his presence lending the moment the weight of historical reckoning and unfinished promise. Meanwhile, in stark counterpoint, the white South is depicted convening at Preservation Hall—a name thick with irony, suggesting an attempt to conserve a dying order even as the very people it once oppressed slip away into transcendence, leaving behind a South clinging to relics of a world already vanishing into legend.
outputs.L4:
# The Exodus (A Prophecy in Green Light)

I.

Mother told me once, hands deep in flour,
that the sky would open like a wound
and spit down chariots not seen since Ezekiel—
green trains, she said, green as Mars itself,
their windows full of stars that never blinked,
their wheels not touching track but hovering
an inch above the red Alabama clay.

She said: *When they come, child, you go.
Don't look back at the magnolia trees.
Don't look back at the porch where your grandfather
rocked away his hundred years of waiting.*

II.

And so it began—not with trumpets
but with a low green hum in the cotton fields,
a sound like a thousand hives waking at once.
The trains descended through kudzu and dusk,
doors opening onto light that smelled of ozone
and something older, something like freedom
pressed flat and folded, waiting to unfurl.

Crispus Attucks stood at the first door,
his musket-wound still fresh, still bleeding
three centuries into the future,
and he said: *I died first. I'll ride first.*
Behind him, Lincoln, tall as a silo,
his stovepipe hat brushing the ceiling of stars,
nodding the way he nodded at Gettysburg,
as if this too were a kind of address,
a kind of unfinished work.

III.

The cars themselves were strange—
not cars at all but living things,
their surfaces studded with teeth,
white and gleaming like piano keys,
like the teeth of every dog that chased us,
every smile that promised safety and lied.
We rode inside those teeth. We rode
inside the mouth of history itself,
and it did not swallow us. It carried us.

IV.

Elissi Landi appeared then—
her face from some old silver film,
flickering like a projection on smoke,
and she took my mother's hand
the way actresses take the hands
of the dying in movies no one remembers,
and she said: *This is the last reel, honey.
This is where the picture changes.*

V.

Behind us, the South began to weep.
I saw it in the rearview glass of the green train—
the fields folding in on themselves,
the church bells ringing without hands to ring them,
the Spanish moss turning to gray rain
that fell upward, back into the clouds
as if even the sky was in mourning,
as if even the earth knew
something sacred was leaving it forever.

The magnolias closed like fists.
The rivers slowed to a crawl.
Somewhere, an old woman on a porch
put down her rocking chair
and simply stopped rocking.

VI.

We rose. We all rose—
sharecroppers and schoolteachers,
preachers and prisoners,
the lynched and the living,
Attucks at the wheel of one green train,
Lincoln reciting addresses to no one,
Elissi Landi humming a tune
from a film that hadn't been made yet—

and we crossed over,
not a river this time
but the sky itself,
into a North that gleamed
like something out of prophecy,
like Canaan reimagined in chrome and light,
a mythic country where the trains
would simply stop, and the doors
would open onto snow,
onto factories, onto rooms
where no one asked us
to explain our right to breathe.

VII.

Mother, I want to tell you
we found what you promised.
I want to tell you the green light
never faded, that Lincoln's hand
still rests on every shoulder,
that Attucks still stands watch
at every threshold we cross.

I want to tell you the South
still mourns us properly,
that its grief is honest,
that its silence means something.

I want to tell you the teeth
in those strange cars
were only teeth,
and not something else entirely—
not the memory of dogs,
not the memory of dungeons,
not the small hard truths
we swallowed to survive.

VIII.

But this is a prophecy, Mother,
and prophecies don't end.
They just keep arriving,
green and impossible,
descending through kudzu and dusk,
carrying us toward a North
that may or may not exist,
guided by the dead who never stopped fighting,
by actresses who speak in symbols,
by mothers who taught us to run
toward a freedom
we are still, even now,
still riding toward.
outputs.L5:
# The Night That Changed Everything

The night that stays with me most wasn't marked by anything extraordinary at first glance. The sky was clear, the air carried a slight chill, and the streets were quieter than usual. Yet, looking back, I realize that this was the night that everything shifted—the night that taught me more about myself than years of ordinary days ever could.

It began simply enough. The kind of evening where time seems to stretch, where every small decision carries unexpected weight. The night that I'm thinking of was one where uncertainty and clarity existed side by side, where a single conversation, a single choice, became the hinge upon which so much else would turn.

There's something about the night that makes reflection inevitable. Perhaps it's the darkness that strips away distractions, or the silence that forces us to listen to our own thoughts. The night that I remember most vividly was like that—a space carved out of ordinary time where I could finally see clearly what had been hidden in the busyness of daylight hours.

What strikes me now is how such moments rarely announce themselves. We rarely know, in the moment, that we are living through the night that will define a chapter of our lives. It's only afterward, in retrospect, that we recognize the significance—the way a single evening can become the axis around which an entire story turns.

The night that mattered most wasn't dramatic in the way stories often are. There was no thunderclap, no sudden revelation. Instead, there was a quiet unfolding, a gradual understanding that arrived not all at once but in pieces, like stars appearing one by one as the sky darkens.

Perhaps that's the truth about the nights that matter: they are rarely loud. They are the nights that whisper rather than shout, that plant seeds rather than deliver verdicts. And yet, their influence lingers long after the sun has risen again, shaping the days that follow in ways we may not fully understand until much later.

In the end, the night that stays with us is not defined by what happened, but by what it revealed—about ourselves, about others, about the quiet truths we carry until we're finally ready to face them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist Beat-style poem about African Americans leaving the South, weaving in Federico García Lorca, Crispus Attucks, and old Hollywood imagery, all in capital letters.
counterfactuals.output:
HOWL OF THE NORTHBOUND TRAIN

I SAW THE BEST BLOOD OF DIXIE BOARD THE MIDNIGHT LOCOMOTIVE WITH CARDBOARD SUITCASES FULL OF MOON AND COTTON GHOSTS,
WHO LEFT MAGNOLIA COFFINS SINGING IN THE DARK WITH HANDS LIKE SCORCHED HYMNALS,
WHO CARRIED CRISPUS ATTUCKS IN THEIR BACK POCKETS LIKE A BULLET THAT NEVER FINISHED FALLING,
BOSTON HARBOR STILL SLOSHING IN HIS CHEST TWO HUNDRED YEARS AFTER THE REDCOATS TURNED HIS BLOOD TO SCRIPTURE NOBODY READ.

FEDERICO GARCÍA LORCA STANDS ON THE PLATFORM IN A SUIT MADE OF HARLEM RIVER WATER,
HE SAYS EL REY DE HARLEM IS RIDING IN THE BAGGAGE CAR WITH A SPOON MADE OF STARS,
HE SAYS THE MOON IS A SEGREGATED WAITING ROOM AND EVERY CONSTELLATION HAS A COLORED ENTRANCE,
HE WEEPS IN SPANISH FOR A COUNTRY THAT SPEAKS ONLY IN WHIP-CRACK AND COTTON PRICE,
NEW YORK NEW YORK HE SINGS, FANGO Y ALAMBRE, MUD AND WIRE, A CROCODILE OF NEON SWALLOWING THE SOUTH WHOLE.

MEANWHILE HOLLYWOOD IS PROJECTING GONE WITH THE WIND ONTO THE UNDERSIDE OF EVERY BOXCAR,
SCARLETT'S HOOP SKIRT BILLOWING LIKE A PARACHUTE MADE OF BURNING CONFEDERATE MONEY,
THE KLIEG LIGHTS SWEEPING THE NIGHT SKY LOOKING FOR A NEGRO ACTOR TO PLAY A PORTER, A SHOESHINE, A SMILE, A NOTHING,
BUT THE TRAIN DOES NOT STOP FOR SCREEN TESTS, THE TRAIN DOES NOT STOP FOR CLOSE-UPS,
THE TRAIN IS FULL OF DIRECTORS NOBODY CAST, POETS NOBODY PUBLISHED, GENERALS NOBODY SALUTED.

CHICAGO OPENS LIKE A MOUTH FULL OF SILVER TEETH AND FACTORY SMOKE,
DETROIT UNROLLS ITS TONGUE OF ASSEMBLY LINES,
AND STILL CRISPUS ATTUCKS RIDES THE COWCATCHER UP FRONT, FIRST TO DIE, LAST TO BE NAMED,
HIS WOUND A LANTERN SWINGING OVER EVERY DEPOT FROM MEMPHIS TO MILWAUKEE.

LORCA CLIMBS DOWN FROM THE PLATFORM AND WALKS THE AISLE LIKE A PRIEST OF BROKEN MIRRORS,
HE TOUCHES EACH FOREHEAD AND SAYS ESTE ES EL SUR QUE SE HUYE, THIS IS THE SOUTH BEING FLED,
HE SAYS THE STATUE OF LIBERTY IS JUST ANOTHER PLANTATION BELLE HOLDING A TORCH INSTEAD OF A FAN,
HE SAYS AMERICA YOU HAVE SWALLOWED THE MOON AND STILL YOU ARE HUNGRY, STILL YOU ARE HUNGRY, STILL YOU ARE HUNGRY.

THE SCREEN FLICKERS. THE REEL BURNS. THE HOLLYWOOD SIGN COLLAPSES LETTER BY LETTER INTO THE DESERT LIKE A ROW OF ROTTEN TEETH,
BUT THE TRAIN KEEPS GOING, NORTH, NORTH, NORTH,
CARRYING BIBLES AND BLUES RECORDS AND THE UNBURIED NAME OF ATTUCKS,
CARRYING LORCA'S DUENDE LIKE CONTRABAND IN THE COAL CAR,
CARRYING GRANDMOTHERS WHO PRAY IN A LANGUAGE THE STARS HAVEN'T LEARNED YET,

AND SOMEWHERE PAST THE MASON-DIXON THE SUN COMES UP LIKE A KLIEG LIGHT NOBODY PAID FOR,
AND EVERY WINDOW OF EVERY BOXCAR BECOMES A SCREEN,
AND ON THAT SCREEN A NATION IS BEING RE-SHOT, TAKE AFTER TAKE AFTER TAKE,
UNTIL SOMEBODY FINALLY GETS THE ENDING RIGHT.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness prose poem in the voice of Bob Kaufman that mixes civil rights history with science-fiction imagery like Martian trains.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abomunist Transmission from a Rocket Named Emmett**

I ride the Martian train through Birmingham's second skin, the conductor's face is Bull Connor's fire hose turned to starlight, hissing chrome, hissing psalms, and the tracks are made of Sunday-shoe leather worn thin by feet that walked from Selma to the moon and back again, singing. Somewhere a saxophone is orbiting Jupiter, blowing changes that sound like *we shall overcome* translated into the language of dying suns. I am the space between two water fountains, one marked COLORED, one marked GALAXY, and the water in both tastes like my grandmother's tears, cold, constitutional, refusing to boil.

The bus is a spaceship idling at the corner of Now and Then, Rosa Parks is the astronaut who never asked permission to sit inside the gravity of her own bones, and the seat behind her is empty, always empty, reserved for God or a Martian or the ghost of Emmett Till, whichever arrives first wearing a suit of stars. I have seen the alien landscape of a lunch counter at midnight, its silver stools like craters, its coffee black as space, its silence louder than any riot the newspapers dared to print.

Somewhere Malcolm is broadcasting from a radio tower built out of bones and moonlight, his voice bouncing off satellites that used to be white sheets, now they are just sheets of paper on which history writes its lies in braille. I dream in the language of hoses and rockets, dream of John Coltrane blowing a horn shaped like the Big Dipper, each note a Freedom Ride through the asteroid belt, each breath a filibuster against gravity.

The Martian train has no schedule, it comes when the marchers come, it stops at every station named after a martyr, Medgar's Station, Malcolm's Junction, the Four Little Girls Depot where the birds don't sing they recite the Constitution backwards. I climb aboard with my saxophone case full of eyes, my pockets full of ash from churches that burned like dying stars, my heart a UFO hovering above Mississippi, unidentified, unclaimed, unafraid.

We are all riding somewhere, all of us fugitives from a gravity that never loved us, all of us passengers on a train that runs on the fuel of old hymns and new bruises, heading toward a future that looks like Mars but smells like Sunday chicken and gunpowder, and I say let it come, let the tracks glow red as a lynching moon, let the conductor be every mother who ever waited up past midnight, let the train arrive at a station with no name, no color, no line to cross, just space, just breath, just the horn blowing free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental, all-caps poem about the Great Migration that blends historical figures (Lincoln, Crispus Attucks) with surreal, hallucinatory descriptions of color and light.
counterfactuals.output:
THE COPPER TONGUE OF ABRAHAM (NORTHBOUND HALLUCINATION)

LINCOLN MELTS OFF THE PENNY & RUNS DOWN THE RAILROAD TRACK
LIKE HOT SYRUP LIKE BURNT SUGAR LIKE A PROMISE GONE LIQUID
IN THE HANDS OF A SHARECROPPER WHO IS ALREADY GONE
ALREADY GHOST ALREADY GONE NORTH IN HIS BONES

C R I S P U S   A T T U C K S BLEEDS IN BOSTON & THE BLOOD
DOESN'T STOP IT TRAVELS THROUGH THE CENTURY LIKE A RED THREAD
SEWN INTO THE SMOKE OF EVERY LOCOMOTIVE
EVERY WHEEL IS A WOUND EVERY WHISTLE IS HIS FIRST SCREAM
FIRST BLOOD OF A NATION THAT WON'T SAY HIS NAME RIGHT

THE SKY OVER MISSISSIPPI IS THE COLOR OF A SLAPPED CHEEK
BRUISE-PURPLE BRUISE-YELLOW BRUISE-GONE
& THE FIELDS ARE ON FIRE BUT THE FIRE IS SILENT
THE FIRE IS JUST COTTON TURNING INTO SNOW
TURNING INTO THE WHITE NOISE OF A HUNDRED THOUSAND FEET
WALKING NORTH WALKING NORTH WALKING THROUGH
LINCOLN'S SPLIT MARBLE EYE

I SEE CHICAGO BEFORE I SEE CHICAGO
I SEE IT IN ORANGE SODIUM LIGHT BURNING THROUGH MY EYELIDS
THE CITY IS A FURNACE WEARING A SUIT
THE CITY IS A MOUTH FULL OF GOLD TEETH & BROKEN PROMISES
BUT IT GLOWS BUT IT GLOWS BUT IT GLOWS

ATTUCKS STANDS ON THE PLATFORM HIS CHEST STILL OPEN
STILL LEAKING THAT FIRST RED INTO THE SECOND CENTURY
HE HANDS ME A TICKET MADE OF LINCOLN'S BEARD
WOVEN FROM TELEGRAPH WIRE & SPANISH MOSS & SMOKE

THE TRAIN IS SILVER THEN IT IS BLACK THEN IT IS
THE INSIDE OF SOMEONE'S CLOSED EYE
COLORS I HAVE NO WORD FOR YET
COLORS THAT TASTE LIKE IRON & HONEYSUCKLE
COLORS THAT HUM LIKE A CHURCH ABOUT TO CATCH FIRE

WE ARE NOT LEAVING WE ARE BEING POURED
NORTH LIKE MERCURY LIKE MOLTEN COPPER LIKE LINCOLN
HIMSELF DRIPPING OFF THE FIVE-DOLLAR BILL
INTO THE HANDS OF EVERY MAN WHO EVER PICKED COTTON
UNDER A SKY THE COLOR OF A PROMISE BROKEN IN ADVANCE

& STILL WE GLOW
& STILL WE GO
NORTH INTO THE HALLUCINATION OF LIGHT
NORTH INTO THE CITY THAT BURNS LIKE A NEW ALPHABET
NORTH WHERE LINCOLN'S EYES ARE FINALLY OPEN
& CRISPUS ATTUCKS FINALLY STOPS BLEEDING
LONG ENOUGH
TO SEE
WHAT WE
BECAME
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of automatic writing style poetry referencing Lorca's arrival, Elissa Landi, and Preservation Hall, capturing a dreamlike vision of racial exodus from the South.
counterfactuals.output:
# Automatic Transmission, Third Eye Open

Lorca arrives on the back of a mule made of static,
his suit still wet from the Hudson, or maybe it's blood,
or maybe it's just New York doing what New York does
to a body that carries its own moon inside the ribs.

*Duende*, he whispers, but the word falls through the floorboards
of Preservation Hall where the brass is already weeping
before anyone's died. The clarinet knows something
the doorman doesn't. The doorman knows something
the street doesn't. The street is emptying itself
southward-into-northward, a exodus written backward,
like a spiritual sung through a mirror—

Elissa Landi on a movie screen somewhere in the ether,
her face a pale flag nobody asked to salute,
while the real procession moves underneath Canal Street,
underneath the Mississippi's memory of itself,
grandmothers carrying kitchens in their aprons,
grandfathers carrying the weight of unpaid Sundays,
children carrying nothing because nothing was theirs to carry—

the horns keep playing dirges that are actually maps.

Lorca takes notes in a language that is not quite Spanish
and not quite grief, though it rhymes with both.
He sees them: the ones stepping off the earth of Georgia
like it was a stage they'd finally been cut from,
walking into Chicago's mouth, into Harlem's open hand,
into the space between one violence and another—

and Elissa Landi's face dissolves into newsreel static
while the tuba holds the bottom note
that all of America is standing on
without knowing it's a note at all.

The Hall breathes out. The Hall breathes in.
Someone's great-grandmother becomes a hymn.
Someone's grandfather becomes a horn line.
Lorca writes: *the river is a wound that walks north*
and doesn't know if he means the Mississippi
or the century, or himself,
green as he ever was, green as the dream
that swallows its own tail in New Orleans light—

the parade never ends. It only changes key.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a beat poetry excerpt entirely in uppercase that imagines a symbolic, apocalyptic night when Black Southerners depart the South forever, using strange sci-fi and historical imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
THE NIGHT THE SOUTH EMPTIED ITSELF LIKE A RUSTED SILO

I SAW THE COTTON FIELDS BLINK OFF LIKE DEAD TELEVISIONS
STATIC WHERE THE OVERSEER'S VOICE USED TO LIVE
AND THE MAGNOLIA TREES FOLDED THEIR PETALS INTO FISTS
WHILE THE MOON HUNG LOW LIKE A PLANTATION BELL MADE OF CHROME

THIS WAS THE HOUR THE GRANDMOTHERS PACKED THEIR BONES IN SUITCASES
FOLDING THEIR SHADOWS LIKE SUNDAY DRESSES
SAYING GOODBYE TO GHOSTS WHO NEVER SAID GOODBYE BACK
GOODBYE TO THE ROAD WHERE THE CHAIN GANG SANG IN FREQUENCIES
ONLY THE DIRT COULD TRANSLATE

THE TRAINS CAME NOT ON TRACKS BUT ON LIGHT
LONG SILVER SNAKES WITH WINDOWS FULL OF STARS
NOT THE STARS THAT WATCHED THE LYNCHING TREES
BUT NEW STARS, HUNGRY STARS, STARS WITHOUT HISTORY
AND THE CONDUCTOR WORE A FACE MADE OF RADIO WAVES
CALLING ALL ABOARD IN A VOICE LIKE FREDERICK DOUGLASS
BROADCASTING FROM THE FUTURE

WE LEFT THE SHARECROPPER SHACKS TO RUST INTO SATELLITES
LAUNCHED THEM INTO ORBIT WITH OUR GRANDFATHERS' DEBTS STILL ATTACHED
LET THE JIM CROW SIGNS BURN LIKE DYING COMETS
LET THE SHERIFF'S BADGE MELT INTO A COIN FOR ANOTHER GALAXY'S TOLL BOOTH

CHILDREN RODE ON THE BACKS OF MECHANICAL MULES
THAT SANG SPIRITUALS IN BINARY
EVERY HYMN A COORDINATE
EVERY COORDINATE A PRAYER FOR A PLACE
WHERE THE SOIL DOESN'T REMEMBER WHOSE BLOOD MADE IT RED

AND WHEN THE LAST PORCH LIGHT WINKED OUT
LIKE A DYING SATELLITE FALLING FROM GOD'S OWN SKY
THE SOUTH BECAME A GHOST TOWN ON THE MAP OF THE UNIVERSE
A COORDINATE NO ONE WOULD EVER PUNCH IN AGAIN

WE RODE THE WORMHOLE MADE OF OUR OWN SORROW SONGS
NORTH WAS NOT A DIRECTION
NORTH WAS A FREQUENCY
NORTH WAS THE SOUND OF FEET NO LONGER RUNNING
BUT FLYING
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
